paras: The bombing of Ebenezer A.M.E. Church in Evanston was a dynamite attack on the night of Friday, May 15, 1903, on the African Methodist Episcopal church of a Black congregation in Evanston, Illinois, a suburb of Chicago. The explosion, set off under the pulpit after the congregation had left, wrecked the interior and front of the building. Papers presented it as the second church bombing in the Chicago area that month and ascribed it either to policy gamblers angered by the pastor's preaching against the game or to Black residents offended by his sermon declaring this "the white man's country"; no one was identified as the bomber.

In the spring of 1903 Black ministers in Chicago were preaching against "policy," a numbers gambling game, and the Associated Press reported that the city's Institutional Church had been wrecked by dynamite after its pastor, R. C. Ransom, preached a sermon against it. Rev. I. N. Daniels, pastor of the African Methodist church at Evanston, approved of Ransom's stand and spoke against policy both at the Institutional Church and from his own pulpit.

In a sermon the week before the bombing, Daniels also told his congregation, according to the Washington Times, that "there were too few real men and women among the negroes" and that this was "the white man's country."

On the night of Friday, May 15, a bomb exploded under the pulpit of the church shortly after the congregation had left the evening service. The Associated Press reported that the interior was demolished and the front of the building blown out, and a second wire version said the blast "could be heard all over Evanston." The Chicago Broad Ax wrote that Daniels "narrowly escaped being caught in the explosion" and that "much damage was done to the building," while the Northwestern Vine described the church as "completely demolished." None of the accounts reports anyone killed or injured.

No arrest appears in the coverage, and the Northwestern Vine attributed the bombing to "some unknown person." The first dispatch gave two motives: that "certain colored people" were incensed by the "white man's country" sermon, or that members, in other versions policy gamblers, were angered by the stand the pastor and a Chicago guest had taken against policy. According to the Washington Times, part of the congregation blamed the anti-policy crusade, while other members believed the pastor's "harsh statements" about the race had given offense.
The Broad Ax reported that some blamed "the policy players, writers, or their friends" and urged "earnest efforts" to bring the perpetrators to justice.

The Associated Press dispatch, dated Chicago, May 15, ran the next day in papers including the Richmond Times-Dispatch, the Salt Lake Herald and the San Antonio Daily Light, and copies continued into late May. Headline writers chose between its two motives: the Salt Lake Herald's "Another Negro Church Wrecked by Policy Players" and the Topeka State Journal's "Because the Pastor Preached Against Policy Game" put the gamblers first. The Washington Times instead led with "Chicago Pastor Had Severely Criticised His Race," and the Gainesville Star's rewrite dropped the policy motive entirely under the headline "Dynamited Because Pastor Said This Was White Man's Country."

In Honolulu the cable shrank the story to one line saying that "two negro churches" had been dynamited "because their ministers preached pro-white sermons," folding the earlier Chicago bombing into the Evanston one.

The Black press treated the bombing as a brief item in local and church columns a week later, and neither the Broad Ax nor the Northwestern Vine mentioned the "white man's country" sermon that several white headlines featured. The Broad Ax found the cause "hard to reason out," and the Northwestern Vine wrote simply "Cause unknown." The Iowa State Bystander remarked that "Dynamite seem to be the fashion in church smashing in Chicago" and suggested that "our colored people had better learn to use dynamite on the southern lynchers when the mobs comes."

The Associated Press and the Broad Ax placed the explosion on Friday night, while the Northwestern Vine said Friday morning. Reports also differ on whether the pastor was in danger: the Broad Ax said he narrowly escaped, whereas the Washington Times and the Indiana Tribüne said the building had already emptied.

bases: A bomb exploded under the pulpit of a Black church, damaging the building; no one was attacked in person and no attackers were identified (A4, A23, A28).
The Associated Press dispatch (A4), a separate wire version (A23) and two Black papers (A28, A29) independently report the dynamiting of the Evanston A.M.E. church on Friday, May 15.

accounts.label: Black correspondents
accounts.gist: An attempt was made to blow up Ebenezer A.M.E.; the pastor narrowly escaped; some blamed policy players (Broad Ax); the church was completely demolished by an unknown person, cause unknown (Northwestern Vine).

framing.detail: Most papers ran the AP dispatch as given, under headlines such as 'Church Wrecked With Dynamite' and 'Bomb Exploded Under a Pulpit'.

Headlines chose a motive: 'Another Negro Church Wrecked by Policy Players' (Salt Lake Herald) and 'Because the Pastor Preached Against Policy Game' (Topeka) versus 'Chicago Pastor Had Severely Criticised His Race' (Washington Times).
The Gainesville Star's rewrite kept only the racial-sermon motive: 'Dynamited Because Pastor Said This Was White Man's Country.'
The Broad Ax called for the perpetrators to feel 'the strong arm of the law'; the Iowa Bystander turned the bombing into a gibe about using dynamite on southern lynchers.
The Northwestern Vine gave a two-sentence notice: 'Cause unknown.'

conflicts.note: The AP 'tonight' under a May 15 dateline and the Broad Ax's 'last Friday night' agree on May 15; the Honolulu 'today' follows a May 16 cable date.
